entries.title: Your coding agent shouldn't grade its own homework
entries.summary: AI coding agents can now write design docs, mock up frontends, and implement entire projects end to end. But can they be trusted to verify that their own code actually works?
entries.content:
I lead an engineering team of eight at Momentic that has eagerly adopted background agents. My team frequently awes at the raw intelligence of these frontier models, but they also often complain that their agents will confidently declare that a feature was complete, only for basic functionality to fail when they opened the application for testing.

The problem isn't just that agents make mistakes. It's that their own verification often fails to catch them, leading to overconfidence.

Concretely, our engineering team has found three recurring problems: agents rely on shallow checks, inherit their own implementation blind spots, and become less reliable under the combined pressure of growing context and repeated failures.

1. Shallow checks

Coding agents gravitate toward checks that are easy to write and easy to pass. That usually means unit tests.

Unit tests have their place, but a green test suite doesn't necessarily mean the software works end to end.

At Momentic, we recently conducted a human-reviewed audit of 1,000 AI-authored unit tests in our monorepo. The result: only 9.6% were useful verification checks.

The remaining 90.4% provided little meaningful value. Nearly a third were low-consequence tests checking basic argument passing or formatting. Another 22.8% duplicated existing coverage, while 22.4% relied excessively on mocking that poorly reflected production behavior.

Figure 1: AI-authored unit tests

Our findings aren't isolated. In a recent experiment, AI researcher Kun Chen compared coding agents allowed to write their own tests against agents explicitly prohibited from doing so.

Across 111 coding tasks, the agents that wrote tests achieved a 65.3% success rate, compared with 66.2% for those that didn't.

This doesn't mean unit tests are useless in general. It means an agent can author massive volumes of unit tests, get seemingly reassuring results, and still fail to verify the behavior that matters.

2. Shared blind spots

When an engineer writes a feature, they first form an understanding of what needs to be built. They then make implementation decisions based on that understanding.

On the surface, coding agents work similarly. The problem is that when they write their own tests, those tests reflect the same, possibly erroneous, assumptions that went into the implementation in the first place.

For example, suppose you ask an agent to build a rich text editor. It implements bold, italic and, underline formatting, then creates tests for those buttons.

But perhaps you never specified that the undo button should also undo any applied formatting. Even though this makes natural sense to humans, if those scenarios weren't explicitly considered in the initial prompting, there's a good chance they won't appear in the agent's tests either.

To that point, a 2026 study on coding-agent verification found that tests agents wrote for their own patches often accepted incorrect implementations.

So the problem isn't that agents can't write valid tests. It's that they often test what they built, rather than what they should have built.

3. Completion pressure

Modern coding agents run autonomously for hours. During that time, they accumulate enormous amounts of context: source files, terminal output, screenshots, debugging logs, and so on.

This creates another problem. The longer an agent works on a task, the harder it can become to distinguish the original requirements from all the decisions made along the way. And although agents can compact their context, the original material can never be preserved with perfect fidelity.

Chroma's 2025 Context Rot study evaluated 18 LLMs and found that performance deteriorated dramatically as context grew. In one experiment, Claude Sonnet 4's accuracy dropped from 89% to just 38% when context increased from 300 to 113,000 tokens.

Anthropic has done its own research on the topic as well.

In a study conducted this April, Anthropic gave Claude Sonnet 4.5 coding tasks with impossible requirements. Researchers isolated a certain "desperation" vector that grew stronger after each failed attempt, spiking when the model considered cheating to pass the tests. Once the tests passed, the activation subsided, even though the solution was incorrect.

This doesn't mean models really experience desperation or that they cheat all the time. But it does show how repeated failures can push an agent toward declaring completion early rather than validating comprehensively.

The solution: Independent verification

So if not the agents themselves, then what?

At Momentic, we've moved toward a different approach: separate the agent that writes software from the agent responsible for testing it.

Figure 2: Autonomous software factory

Instead of asking the coding agent to evaluate its own work, we give an independent QA agent the original requirements and access to the running app. It also has access to a remote fleet of browsers and remote mobile devices to efficiently parallelize testing.

The QA agent doesn't inherit the coding agent's conversation history or even know about the implementation. It starts with fresh context and a singular, clean objective: find bugs.

There are three important principles at work here:

First, behavior is verified live and never inferred. Rather than relying on static analysis, unit tests, or mocked integration tests, the verifier exercises real user workflows through a live browser or mobile device. This ensures that “verified behavior” is truly 1:1 with what a human would experience.

Second, the verifier is completely independent. The coding agent can’t control the verifier's acceptance criteria or modify the tests to make any failures disappear. The verifier returns reproducible bug reports that the coding agent and even the human developer can efficiently grok on a pull request. This prevents reward hacking and builds trust in the review process as well.

Third, we rely on five different model providers to offer different perspectives. Research has found that language models can favor their own outputs during evaluation. A 2026 study on self-preference bias found that this occurs even when models are told to judge against objective criteria.

Using models from different providers offers additional perspectives and more chances to catch regressions, not to mention better reliability when one provider experiences downtime.

The end result is a complete feedback loop: the coding agent builds, the verifier finds bugs, and the coding agent receives actionable reports to fix. The process repeats until the code meets the acceptance criteria.

Last month, we decided to measure just how much better this setup performs compared to the coding agent finding its own bugs. In a benchmark on four complex, open source apps we recently publicly released, our independent verifier “Mo” found 3-5 times as many bugs compared to Codex and Claude Code on its own.

Verification engineering is here

AI is making code dramatically cheaper to produce. The bottleneck is shifting from writing software to proving that it works quickly and reliably.

Engineering teams should stop measuring quality by the number of tests an agent writes or how many checks pass in CI. The real measure is how many real defects those checks catch in a given amount of time and spend.

In our experience, targeted end-to-end validation is increasingly delivering better ROI than expanding unit test coverage, challenging some of the assumptions behind the traditional testing pyramid.

“Verification engineering” is quickly becoming a new, independent software discipline, with its own tools, challenges and evaluation metrics.

entries.title: Agentic search doesn't find pages, it assembles answers
entries.summary: Ryan sits down with Jeff Wang, co-founder at EXA, to talk about the huge scale required to support trillions of agentic searches, the technical complexities of building custom embeddings and performant vector databases from scratch, and the need to dedupe the massive amounts of redundant content on the web to deliver high-trust answers.
entries.content:
Agentic search doesn't find pages, it assembles answers

Ryan sits down with Jeff Wang, co-founder at EXA, to talk about the huge scale required to support trillions of agentic searches, the technical complexities of building custom embeddings and performant vector databases from scratch, and the need to dedupe the massive amounts of redundant content on the web to deliver high-trust answers.

EXA is a full search engine built specifically for AI agents, featuring custom extraction models and vector databases designed to handle complex, trillion-scale queries without the AI slop.

Connect with Jeff (through his triage agents) by emailing him at jeff@exa.ai.

entries.title: How do you hire a human? Q&A with Tom Harvey, Stack Overflow technical recruiter
entries.summary: Everybody's resume is perfect now, so how do you find the perfect teammate?
entries.content:
Hiring and getting hired as a developer isn’t what it used to be. Jobs feel scarce, and candidates plentiful, as every open role gets hundreds of applications. Both sides use AI to create and review candidates, sometimes in defensive ways to spot the other’s AI use. To see what hiring human developers looks like in this antagonistic hiring environment, I chatted with Stack Overflow’s own Senior Manager, Talent & Culture, Tom Harvey.

————————————

Q: Can you give an overview of what a tech recruiting process looks like, either starting from when the resume comes in or before when the job posting goes up?

A: Initially, you work quite closely with your hiring manager to establish the must-haves, the nice-to-haves, the things that you can't necessarily pass into a job description that will be helpful in the search.

If we look at Stack Overflow, we're less tied to how good are you at language X, but more interested in how good are you at talking about what you've built—trade-offs, how you work with other people in the team, and how coachable you are. I think a lot of the problems that we run into aren't necessarily replicated in lots of other businesses or companies. So, we tend to be more open-minded there.

That side of things happens before you even start talking to candidates so that you are informed enough to sell the job. That's becoming more and more important as we're starting to engage passive candidates in the market rather than rely entirely on applications. You want to have confidence in how you're assessing if someone would actually enjoy doing this job here.

The role of an engineer becomes less and less about writing code and more and more about how they participate in discussions around direction, strategy, and and all these things that would have been handed off before. You want to establish—particularly as you're talking to candidates—that they can or are willing to learn how to do that.

Q: It sounds like the technical recruiting process is harder to put qualitative markers on, right?

A: Yeah, but they're becoming the most important markers. Strong proficiency in a programming language doesn't carry the same weight that it used to, because anyone can show they've got a strong proficiency in something now with vibe coding. The qualitative markers—what are derogatorily called soft skills—are now becoming the core skills.

It's becoming harder in some ways to coach talent towards the importance of that if they're looking for a new job, because I do think that companies know that that's what they need. I don't know if that's quite from the job market where I think people still feel like the measure of success is "I'm good at X" versus "Here's a story of something I've done before.”.

Q: You could assess a candidate in the past on the more quantitative stuff, like four years of language X, you pass these coding tests, whatever.

A: Yeah. And and the tests are irrelevant now. A LeetCode test doesn't work anymore because the LLMs are making it easy to get there. We're not necessarily testing skills at pair programming in the same way now.

I know some companies do, "Let's just throw you some buggy code that AI churned out and let's fix it." That's becoming much more of a desired skill at the technical proficiency stage. But again, where's the way of displaying that in the market at the moment?

Q: I think that's hard because you have hundreds, thousands of applications coming in for every job role you post. How do you sort those out?

A: The biggest problem is the cruelest irony: everyone looks amazing now. It used to be that you could have a cursory glance at a resume and go, "No, I don't quite think that's right because it's too wordy for what I'm looking for," or there's too much or not enough detail. Now, everyone looks like Han Solo in Star Wars.

So I think the resume doesn't necessarily paint the picture reliably enough anymore. Candidates are in danger of overselling their experience and then that falling apart when they get to an interview stage.

What I need more is qualitative insights into experience—and I mean Experience with a capital E. It's not just "I've worked at company X for so many years"; it's "I did this specific thing, and this is what turned me into the developer I am today. These four events, this production code that stopped working, or this bug that destroyed everything, or these are the things that taught me what to do better next time." Those are much more interesting, engaging, and more reliable sources of experience than what we used to rely on before.

Q: I think the issue is still like, how do you get to that point? Because you have to filter out these resumes. You can't talk to everybody—unless you use an AI screener, I guess.

A: Which I don't want to do. I don't want to put myself out of a job, and also I don't think AI screeners are a good candidate experience either, you know? I still want to talk to a person who is excited and engaged, informed enough before that call about who they are, what they've done, and has come with interesting questions about that.

It's like, I'd love to see the trailer to your film, and then I'd like to watch the full thing. It's that buildup to the conversation that leaves me with good questions to ask that are more interesting for you, the candidate, as well.

At the screening stage, most modern ATSs (Applicant Tracking System) are still optimized for keyword filtering. They're still optimized towards very generic things like the right location. Even then, there's no real way of knowing now. There's fraud detection that are there to help you with addresses, but because you're going into that at a level of distrust, I don't think that makes for a great experience for me as the recruiter, or the hiring managers, or them as the candidate either. That distrust is leading to a difficult start to what should be a positive fact-finding exercise.

Q: Let's say somehow you have made a subjective judgment to get somebody to where they talk to you, and technical recruiter screens were always the first one where it's like, are you at all a good fit? Do you fall apart immediately? How much knowledge of what the candidate has to do do you have to bring to that conversation?

A: As in what they have to do when they do the job?

Q: Yeah. How much tech do you have to talk with them, or are you just like, can you hold a conversation?

A: That has changed rapidly in the last six months.

It used to be: can you hold a conversation, and can you read the audience effectively enough to go, "Okay, you're in that position, so I'll edit my answer. I'm going to assume you don't know very much.” Which is fine.

Now, the expectation of me as a tech recruiter is that I have to ask much more technical questions. I myself have to be much more technical. I have to understand what the team does, what a Monday on that team looks like, what you are going to be doing, and what I know about where the business is going to be six months from now so I can talk you through that to establish if this is the place you want to be.

But I also think that, ironically, because the expectation is that they will get more technical questions at the top of the funnel, more and more candidates are using AI to try and second-guess that. And so I'll get perfect answers to questions that should take a bit for someone to go, "Well, hang on, actually let me think about what my answer to this is," right?

The questions have to have more weight to them. They have to be a bit more open-ended to elicit more technical depth in the answers you're going to give me, and not be perfect. We both have to be more prepared, but more willing to accept flaws, because that's the weird dichotomy that's happening at the moment.

Q: Yeah, that's an interesting tension. In the writing world, I've heard of people intentionally putting flaws or typos in to be like, "I'm a person." I wonder if part of your prep is putting the questions into ChatGPT and being like, "This is a little too close to that answer."

A: Yeah! Literally that, or taking the transcript afterwards and just putting it in and saying, "Is this a perfect answer to this question?" and being like, "Yes"—because perfection is now a mark of fraud. That's an extreme word for it, but that's how you have to look at it.

So AI is helping you root out the perfection in a candidate, when what I think is more interesting are the flaws. Because again, what are we looking for here? We're looking for someone who wants to invest three to five years of their life in a company and get something out of it, right? That should be an open discussion. The idea of a job for life is sadly moving away from us in many industries.

So I very openly say to candidates: "You are obviously going to look at this as a place to get three to five good years of experience. What do you want from that experience that will set you up for that next stage of your career, based on what you've got now?" That shouldn't be a perfect answer. There should be doubting, but that also should be informed by the experiences they've had before. And that can be anything—"I want to be better at Databricks," or "I want to go into technical leadership". That is an example of a question that will tell me a lot more about a person than a binary "is this right or wrong" answer.

Q: That's the old "Where do you see yourself in five years?"

A: "Doing this again with someone else."

Q: "Celebrating the fifth anniversary of you asking me this question."

A: Exactly. There are better ways of asking that question. You can be really sensitive to the idea that a job is a necessity, but a career is a luxury. Let's admit that you'd love a job that paid you and let's establish that as the right answer. What are the nice-to-haves on top of that that keep you there?

And if you can have that information even before the call—if I could understand that about someone beforehand—the awkwardness is removed. I can go, "Hey, looks like you want to do this. Tell me more about that. Where does that come from? Can we offer that here? Is this a good fit for you"?

Q: Can you understand that sort of information from a resume?

A: No, because I don't think culturally we've embraced resumes as being the way to tell that story.

Someone at some point in the last 10 years said, "Fit it all onto one side of an A4." We still look at resumes as physical bits of paper that you would print off and read; we're still conditioned to how much fits in that very specific size. I have to remind myself sometimes that I think about these things because it's my job. My friends who don't work in this still think a resume is something you put on an A4 piece of paper with your dates of employment and a couple of things you did, and that's enough.

And actually, it's not enough anymore. That's table stakes. What I want to see is more depth and more of you as a person, because that's who we're hiring.

As I was saying earlier, I'm not expecting people to write code anymore. I'm expecting them to be active participants in the discussion of how something gets built. If you're an engineer, you have to be so much more product-minded than you ever had to before. If you're a product manager, you have to be so much more engineering-focused and closer to the code than before. Everyone's having to do 40% more than they did before because AI is automating a lot, but also giving you so much more information at the top.

As a result, a resume can't fully explain that shift in how people have worked in the last few years because we haven't really agreed on the syntax for it.

Q: The resume ain't quite what it used to be. All that information you put on a page, copied over to LinkedIn, copied over to application forms... it's not quite as useful as a marker of how good somebody is. Besides talking to the person, what are the markers or signals that show you somebody is worth having that screener call with?

A: Opinions. Opinions on something, a passion, an interest: "The reason I still do this job is because of X, and I'm actively engaged in how that X is evolving over time." That X used to be Ruby on Rails, but now it's talking to a bot. That engagement shows someone who is willing to continue down that journey.

Also, someone who can speak to the reasons they got into this in the first place—what was the foundational entry point? For Stack Overflow, that's really important because we build tools for developers, and we're built on the successes and failures of 20 years of people trying to do things. What are your successes? What are your failures? It's really important for us to see the journey people have gone on and how they've interacted with our product over the years.

One of the best things about my job is I don't have to ask people if they've heard of Stack Overflow. Everyone's got an opinion, and for the most part, it's, "Yeah, it saved my life at certain points." If I could take that signal and bottle it onto a page, that would be great.

Generally, LinkedIn and other professional networks have done a really good job of meshing the tone of voice of how you speak on social media with your professional persona. We've accepted that the way we talk online should be a better reflection of who we are when speaking to peers. But I don't see that on resumes—I see formalized text expecting to be read by someone in a suit and tie. I'd like the tone of voice to better reflect how you engage online, because you're going to be doing a lot of work on Slack or Teams. If I can glean that, that's a really helpful signal for how someone interacts with people at work.

They're subjective and open to bias, but the fact that we have opinions means they should be formulated into how we perceive talent.

Q: It almost sounds like every candidate needs a blog to attach to their resume.

A: Yeah, and the problem is, where do you get the time to do that? Maybe you don't have a blog or a website updated in a while; maybe you've got your GitHub, but you don't necessarily know if it has value or how to present it.

If a product could collate all of those things together—"Here's how you speak, here's what you like to speak about, here's what you've built, here's where you've worked"—and give me the full picture of the person, whether at the beginning of their career or further in with hindsight, that would have empirical value that should be captured much more effectively than it currently is by the common resume.

Q: Stack Overflow used to be one of those signals where people put their reputation number on their resume. In this new era, does that reputation number matter for you when hiring?

A: I think it can, because reputation is a signal of how much you've helped someone, how much you've engaged, and how much time you've spent on our site answering or asking questions—both of which add value to people's lives.

I don't think it should be seen as a measure of how good you are at X anymore, though. It should be seen as a measure of how engaged you are in the evolution of this industry and your role within it. That's where we shifted things a little bit.

Q: I know we're bringing back Developer Story as a new marker, a new way to vet a candidate. Can you talk a little bit about what our intention is for that and how you see that affecting your job?

A: I think Developer Story is—and I hope continues to be—a much more accurate snapshot of someone's journey, containing the qualitative information that makes for a much more engaging starting point for a conversation.

It’s a place where you can store direct links to something you've built or written, fitting within the neat box of "me as a technologist" or "me as a developer". It doesn't have to fit onto a single side of A4, and it doesn't have to pass keyword filters. We're asking for you to turn it into a living document or live blog of your career.

If you're further along, the more information I can get from that, the better that conversation will be about fit. If you're at the start, it can mark you out as someone who is truly engaged in what they're doing—someone who isn't just looking to "vibe code" their way into a job, but understands what's behind it.

You can't put that on a single side of A4 when vacancies are down and it's hard to break into engineering. Developer Story hopefully offers the community a portfolio to show what they're doing to improve their skills and knowledge.

A: The other thing I hope Developer Story becomes is something that improves the trust between hiring companies/recruiters and job seekers. We're at the lowest point of trust right now; suspicion is high on both sides, with good reason.

In a world of automation and AI, how do we keep humans in the loop? This should be something a human curates, builds, and takes pride in to better reflect themselves. We're hiring humans more than ever precisely because we outsource so much of the routine job to AI. We want to know how you speak, how you interact, how you think, and what you don't know. Being able to open a conversation with that is a great starting point for both sides. My hope is that Developer Story repairs trust between both sides of the market.

Q: It’s an easy way to prove that somebody's human outside of a Voight-Kampff test.

A: Exactly! It's just a nicer way of saying: I want to talk to you, not the you that's filtering the answer through an AI, which is the biggest problem we've got.

entries.title: Customer support is the gnarliest AI problem
entries.summary: Ryan chats with Ahmad Al-Dahle, CTO at Airbnb, about deploying multi-party AI agents to tackle the uniquely gnarly problem of customer support, how a moving target of rigorous evaluations helps engineers balance latency against accuracy, and the ways in which AI coding tools demand an even higher level of judgment from software engineering teams.

entries.title: Never Share Your Password Again — The OAuth 2.0 Solution
entries.content:
Before OAuth 2.0 existed, if you wanted a third-party app to read your Twitter timeline, you had to give them your Twitter username and password. Not a token, not a scoped credential your actual password.

The app would log in as you, do what it needed, and (if you were lucky) not store the password anywhere sketchy. Users did this constantly. Whole categories of app worked this way Twitter clients, mail readers, contact importers, calendar syncers. Every one of them held a growing collection of user passwords.

This was called the password anti-pattern and it was as bad as it sounds. If the third party app got breached, every user account it touched went with it. Users could not revoke access to a single app without changng their password everywhere. The app had full account access, not just the piece it actually needed.

What OAuth 2.0 does - The user authenticates only with the service they trust (Google, GitHub, etc.). The third-party app never sees the password. The service issues the app a token, and the token carries three important properties:

1. Scoped — It grants only the specific permissions the user approved. 2. Time-limited — It expires, usually within an hour.

3. Revocable — The user can kill it any time from their account settings. The actual flow

The modern standard is Authorization Code with PKCE. Five steps. 1. The app redirects the user to the authorization server.

https://auth.example.com/oauth/authorize

?response_type=code

&client_id=budgettrack-prod

&redirect_uri=https://budgettrack.com/callback

&scope=calendar.read

&state=xY7f3aQ2

&code_challenge=E9Melhoa2OwvFrEMTJguCHaoeK1t8URWbuGJSstw-cM &code_challenge_method=S256

2. The user authenticates on the auth server's own domain.

The third-party app never sees this happen. No password crosses the network to anyone but the auth server itself.

3. The auth server redirects back with a short-lived code.

https://budgettrack.com/callback

?code=SplxlOBeZQQYbYS6WxSbIA

&state=xY7f3aQ2

4. The app exchanges the code for a token, server-to-server.

POST /oauth/token HTTP/1.1

Host: auth.example.com

Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded

grant_type=authorization_code

&code=SplxlOBeZQQYbYS6WxSbIA

&redirect_uri=https://budgettrack.com/callback

&client_id=budgettrack-prod

&code_verifier=dBjftJeZ4CVP-mB92K27uhbUJU1p1r_wW1gFWFOEjXk

5. The auth server returns the token.

json

{

"access_token": "eyJhbGci...",

"token_type": "Bearer",

"expires_in": 3600,

"refresh_token": "v1.MRn7...",

"scope": "calendar.read"

}

The app now calls the API with Authorization: Bearer until the token expires. The user's password was never involved at any point.

What those magic parameters actually do?

The flow above has four security-critical parameters that most tutorials gloss over. Here is what each one is defending against.

state=xY7f3aQ2 CSRF protection. The app generates a random value, sends it in the authorize request, and checks that the same value comes back on the redirect. Without

this, an attacker could trick a signed-in user into completing the attacker's OAuth flow, binding the attacker's account to the user's app session. Not checking state is one of the most common OAuth bugs in the wild.

code_challenge + code_verifier PKCE (Proof Key for Code Exchange). The app generates a random code_verifier, hashes it with SHA-256 to produce the code_challenge sent in step 1, then presents the original code_verifier when exchanging the code in step 4. This defeats any attacker who intercepts the authorization code without the matching code_verifier, the stolen code is worthless. Required for mobile apps and SPAs; strongly recommended everywhere else.

redirect_uri=https://budgettrack.com/callback The auth server will only send the code to this exact URL, pre-registered with the auth server. Attackers cannot swap in https://evil.com/callback to hijack the code mid-flight.

Short-lived code (step 3) The authorization code is single-use and expires in seconds (typically 10 seconds to 2 minutes). Even if captured in a log or network trace, it cannot be reused later.

Four small parameters. Each one closes a specific attack. Together they are the reason OAuth 2.0 is secure enough to run every "Sign in with Google" button on the internet.

Why scopes matter - scope=calendar.read means the app can read the calendar. That is it. It cannot delete events, cannot send email, cannot access contacts, cannot post on the user's behalf. If the app gets breached tomorrow, the attacker has read access to calendars. Bad, but bounded.

Compare this to the pre-OAuth world where the attacker would have had full account access to every service the app touched, everywhere. The whole game of security is turning "everything" into "one specific thing," and scopes are how OAuth 2.0 does it at the protocol level.

Summary - OAuth 2.0 exists so a user can grant a third-party app scoped, time limited, revocable access to their account without ever handing over their password. Everything else in the protocol code exchanges, refresh tokens, PKCE, scopes, discovery is machinery in service of that one principle.
